Q: robots.txt allow root only, disallow everything else? A:

Important: If you're using a sitemap, you need to explicitly allow it too!

The accepted answer is correct for blocking everything except the root. However, there's a common pitfall: if you have a sitemap.xml, it will also be blocked by Disallow: /.

I ran into this issue with Google Search Console showing "Sitemap could not be read - General HTTP error" even though the sitemap was accessible via browser.

The fix is to explicitly allow your sitemap:

User-agent: *
Allow: /$
Allow: /sitemap.xml
Disallow: /

Sitemap: https://www.example.com/sitemap.xml

The Sitemap: directive at the bottom tells crawlers where your sitemap is, but they still need permission to fetch it. Since Disallow: / blocks all paths, you must add Allow: /sitemap.xml before the disallow rule.

Q: Latency of assembly memory ops in modern CPUs A:

The c9x.me pages are mostly scraped from some old version1 of Intel's vol.2 PDF, but the latency/throughput numbers are added by someone, for very old CPUs, I think Pentium 4 hence the half-cycle latency for mov reg, reg.

See https://agner.org/optimize for numbers on newer CPUs reg-reg vs. memory mov, but note that his instruction table's load latency numbers are just part of arbitrarily dividing store/reload latency between stores and loads, and are not actually L1d-hit load-use latency.
Agner Fog's microarch guide is very good background for understanding what to do with these numbers, though.

See https://uops.info/ for good experimental test results on Intel up to about Alder Lake, and AMD up to Zen 4, which do test load-use latency (for L1d hits, like mov rax, [rax] with a pointer that points to itself). For ops like movdqa where the result can't directly be used in the next addressing-mode, they invent a chain like movdqa xmm0, [rax] / movq rax, xmm0 and assume 1c latency for other ops in the chain to get an upper bound on latency, but we know that's overly pessimistic and the real latency is a bit less.

With some clever analysis, it can be possible to figure out the exact latency of an instruction like movq rax, xmm0 and thus know the actual chain latency.

In practice yes 6 cycles is about right on most CPUs for SIMD loads, or 7 cycles for 256-bit or 512-bit loads. CPU vendors sometimes publish numbers for these in their optimization manuals, and/or in technical presentations about their newest generation of CPU design and stuff like that.

For loads that miss in L1d cache, there are multiple outer levels of cache. Modern x86 CPUs have per-core private L2, so L2 hit latency is a fixed number of cycles, but L3 has to go off-core, with latency depending on the interconnect (much worse for Intel's big many-core CPUs with one big unified L3 per socket; less bad on AMD Zen where clusters of cores have their own L3.)

See articles like https://chipsandcheese.com/p/lion-cove-intels-p-core-roars and https://chipsandcheese.com/p/amds-ryzen-9950x-zen-5-on-desktop for benchmarks of memory latency, and inter-core latency for loading a value that's in MESI "Modified" state in another core's L1d cache, so it has to get written back to L3 first, or otherwise transfered.

L3 miss latency also depends on DRAM timings (and whether the DRAM "page" containing the cache line is already open), and potentially even how much competition there is from other cores and/or the iGPU. See How much of ‘What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory’ is still valid?
For some real numbers under good conditions (single-threaded workload), see for example https://www.7-cpu.com/cpu/Zen3.html where they measured DRAM latency as 47 cycles + 74 ns on a specific system. Also with info on TLB misses for the L1dTLB and second level TLB.

Footnote 1: I normally use https://www.felixcloutier.com/x86/, which is scraped from Intel's vol.2 PDF as of 2024-02-18 so has newer instructions, and incorporates more fixes for mistakes in older versions of the manual. The performance info on the c9x.me pages is so old it's completely irrelevant.
